chapter.title: Pointers, windows and binary search
chapter.summary: Three patterns that turn O(n²) scans into O(n) or O(log n) by exploiting order and locality.

lessons.title: Two pointers
lessons.summary: Walk two indexes through the data so each element is handled once, instead of checking every pair.

parts.label: Concept
parts.body:
## The idea

Many array problems look like they need to compare every pair of elements, which is `O(n²)`. If the data has **structure** (usually *sorted*), you can keep **two indexes** and move them intelligently so you only pass over the array once: **O(n)**.

There are two main shapes.

## Shape 1: opposite ends, moving inward

Put `left` at the start and `right` at the end. Each step, look at the pair and decide which pointer to move.

**Example: Two Sum on a sorted array.** Target 9, array `[1, 3, 4, 6, 8, 11]`.

| left | right | sum | action |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 11 | 12 | too big, so move `right` left (a smaller number is the only way to reduce the sum) |
| 1 | 8 | 9 | found |

**Why it is correct:** if `a[left] + a[right]` is too big, then `a[right]` is too big for **every** remaining left partner (they are all at least `a[left]`), so `right` can be discarded safely. Symmetrically for too small. Each step discards one element, so at most `n` steps.

Other problems of this shape: valid palindrome, container with most water, 3Sum (fix one number, two-pointer the rest, giving `O(n²)` instead of `O(n³)`), reversing an array in place.

## Shape 2: same direction (read and write, or slow and fast)

Both start at the left. The **fast** pointer scans; the **slow** pointer marks where the next result goes.

**Example: remove duplicates from a sorted array in place.** `slow` points at the last unique value written; `fast` scans ahead. When `a[fast] != a[slow]`, increment `slow` and copy.

This is also how you remove all zeros, partition around a pivot, or compact an array with `O(1)` extra space.

**Fast and slow on a linked list** (Floyd's cycle detection): fast moves 2 steps, slow moves 1. If there is a cycle they must meet; the middle of a list is where slow stands when fast reaches the end.

## When to reach for two pointers

- The array is **sorted**, or can be sorted without hurting (sorting costs `O(n log n)`).
- You need a **pair or triple** satisfying a condition.
- You must **modify in place** with `O(1)` space.
- The problem is about a **palindrome** or **symmetry**.

## Pitfalls

- **Skip duplicates** in 3Sum or you will output repeated triples.
- Use `left < right`, not `<=`, when pairing two different elements.
- Two pointers on **unsorted** data usually does not work. Use a hash map instead.
- Off-by-one on the loop condition. Test with 0, 1 and 2 elements.

diagrams.code:
flowchart LR

  B --> C["left=0 right=4: 1+8=9 match"]

keyPoints: Two pointers replace a nested pair search with one pass, usually on sorted data.
Opposite-end pointers discard one element per step because order proves it cannot pair.
Same-direction (read/write) pointers compact or partition an array in place in O(1) space.
3Sum = sort, fix one element, two-pointer the rest, skipping duplicates.
On unsorted data prefer a hash map; two pointers needs structure.

check.q: In sorted two-sum, sum is larger than the target. Which pointer moves, and why?
options: left moves right, to grow the sum
right moves left, because a[right] is too big for every remaining partner
check.why: Every remaining left partner is at least a[left], so a[right] overshoots with all of them and can be discarded.

check.q: What is the extra space of the read/write two-pointer duplicate removal?
check.why: It overwrites the input array using two indexes and allocates nothing else.

options: It enables the two-pointer scan for the remaining pair and makes duplicates adjacent to skip
check.why: Sorted order drives the two-pointer logic and groups equal values so duplicate triples can be skipped.

lessons.title: Sliding window
lessons.summary: Maintain a moving range over a sequence, updating the answer incrementally instead of recomputing it for each position.

parts.label: Concept
parts.body:
## The idea

Problems about a **contiguous subarray or substring** ("longest substring with...", "max sum of k consecutive...") invite a brute force of `O(n²)` (try every start and end) or worse. A **sliding window** keeps a range `[left, right]` and, as it moves one step, **updates** its summary (sum, counts) rather than recomputing from scratch.

## Fixed-size window

Window length is a constant `k`. Slide it by adding the entering element and removing the leaving one.

**Example: maximum sum of k consecutive elements.** For `[2, 1, 5, 1, 3, 2]`, `k = 3`:

| window | sum |
|---|---|
| 2,1,5 | 8 |
| 1,5,1 | 8 - 2 + 1 = 7 |
| 5,1,3 | 7 - 1 + 3 = 9 |
| 1,3,2 | 9 - 5 + 2 = 6 |

One pass, `O(n)`. Each step is a constant update, not a fresh sum of `k` numbers.

## Variable-size window

The window **grows** by moving `right`, and **shrinks** from `left` whenever it becomes invalid. This template solves most such problems:

```
left = 0
for right in 0..n-1:
    add a[right] to the window state
    while window is invalid:
        remove a[left] from the state
        left += 1
    update best answer using window [left, right]
```

**Example: longest substring without repeating characters.** State = a set (or map of last-seen index) of characters in the window. When `s[right]` is already inside, shrink from the left until it is not, then record `right - left + 1`.

**Why it is O(n):** `right` moves `n` times and `left` moves at most `n` times in total. Even though there is a `while` inside the `for`, each element enters and leaves the window once: at most `2n` steps.

## Choosing what the window stores

- **A running sum**: for sum constraints (works with positive numbers; negatives break the "shrink when too big" logic).
- **A set**: uniqueness.
- **A frequency map**: "at most k distinct", "contains all letters of t" (minimum window substring), anagram in a string.
- **A deque**: sliding window maximum, keeping candidates in decreasing order.

## Longest vs shortest

- **Longest valid window**: expand, shrink only when invalid, record after fixing.
- **Shortest valid window**: expand until valid, then shrink *while it stays valid*, recording each time.

## Pitfalls

- Updating the answer **before** the window is valid again.
- Forgetting to remove the element at `left` from the state when shrinking (a map count must decrement, and delete at zero).
- Using a sliding window when numbers can be **negative** and the constraint is a sum. Use prefix sums and a hash map instead.
- Returning window size off by one: length is `right - left + 1`.

diagrams.title: Window grows with right, shrinks with left, each index visited at most twice
diagrams.code:
flowchart LR
  A["expand: right++"] --> B{"window valid?"}
  B -- "yes" --> C["record best"] --> A
  B -- "no" --> D["shrink: left++"] --> B

code.source:
# Fixed window: max sum of k consecutive elements. O(n)
def max_sum_k(nums, k):
    s = sum(nums[:k])
    best = s
    for i in range(k, len(nums)):
        s += nums[i] - nums[i - k]
        best = max(best, s)
    return best

# Variable window: longest substring without repeating characters. O(n)
def length_of_longest_substring(s):
    seen = set()
    left = best = 0
    for right, ch in enumerate(s):
        while ch in seen:
            seen.remove(s[left])
            left += 1
        seen.add(ch)
        best = max(best, right - left + 1)
    return best

keyPoints: A window is a contiguous range whose summary is updated incrementally as it slides.
Fixed windows add the entering and remove the leaving element; variable windows expand right and shrink left.
Total work is O(n) even with a while inside the for: each index enters and leaves once.
Choose the window state to match the constraint: sum, set, frequency map or deque.
Negative numbers break sum-based shrinking; use prefix sums with a hash map instead.

check.q: Why is the variable sliding window O(n) despite a while loop inside the for loop?
options: left only moves forward, so each element is added and removed at most once
check.why: Both pointers move forward only: at most n advances of right plus n of left, so 2n steps.

check.q: Which pattern would you use for the *shortest* subarray that satisfies a condition?
options: Expand until valid, then shrink while it stays valid, recording each time
check.why: For shortest, you record while the window is valid and keep shrinking to find the smallest valid one.

check.q: Why can a sliding window fail on 'subarray sum equals k' with negative numbers?
options: Adding elements no longer always increases the sum, so you cannot tell when to shrink
Negatives are not allowed in arrays
check.why: The window logic assumes growing makes the sum bigger and shrinking makes it smaller. Negatives break that monotonicity.

lessons.title: Binary search
lessons.summary: Halve the search space each step, on sorted arrays and, more powerfully, on any yes/no answer that flips once.

parts.label: Concept
parts.body:
## The idea

Guess a number from 1 to 1000. The best strategy: guess 500; I say "higher" or "lower"; you discard half the range every time. After **10 guesses** (`log₂ 1000 ≈ 10`) you are done. Linear search could take 1000.

**Binary search finds a target in a sorted array in `O(log n)`**: each comparison throws away half of the remaining candidates.

## The template (learn this one and stick to it)

```
lo = 0, hi = n - 1
while lo <= hi:
    mid = lo + (hi - lo) // 2      # avoids overflow in fixed-width ints
    if a[mid] == target: return mid
    if a[mid] < target:  lo = mid + 1
    else:                hi = mid - 1
return -1
```

- **Invariant:** if the target exists, it is within `[lo, hi]`.
- Each step shrinks the range by at least one (`mid ± 1`), so the loop always ends.
- When the loop ends, `lo > hi`: the range is empty and the target is absent. `lo` is then the **insertion point** (where the target *would* go).

## Walkthrough

Search 7 in `[1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11]`:

| lo | hi | mid | a[mid] | action |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | 5 | 2 | 5 | 5 < 7, lo = 3 |
| 3 | 5 | 4 | 9 | 9 > 7, hi = 3 |
| 3 | 3 | 3 | 7 | found |

## Beyond "find the value": search on a boundary

The most useful form finds the **first position where a condition becomes true**, in a sequence like `F F F F T T T T`. Template:

```
lo = 0, hi = n              # hi is one past the end
while lo < hi:
    mid = lo + (hi - lo) // 2
    if condition(mid): hi = mid     # mid might be the answer
    else:              lo = mid + 1
return lo                           # first true (or n if none)
```

This single pattern gives you **lower bound** (first index `>= x`), **upper bound**, first/last occurrence, insertion position, and first bad version.

## Binary search on the answer

The array does not have to exist. If you can answer **"is X big enough?"** monotonically (small X: no, large X: yes), binary search over the *range of possible answers*.

**Example: Koko eating bananas.** Piles `[3, 6, 7, 11]`, must finish in `h = 8` hours. Find the smallest eating speed `k`. For a candidate `k`, hours needed = sum of `ceil(pile / k)`. That is monotone: faster speed never needs more hours. Search `k` between 1 and the largest pile. Cost: `O(n log M)` where `M` is the largest pile.

The same trick solves: ship packages within D days, split array largest sum, minimum capacity problems, square root, and "smallest value such that...".

## Rotated sorted arrays

In `[4, 5, 6, 7, 0, 1, 2]` one half of any range is always sorted. Check which half is sorted, test whether the target lies in it, and discard the other half. Still `O(log n)`.

## Pitfalls

- **Infinite loop** when you set `lo = mid` or `hi = mid` in the `lo <= hi` template. Always move past `mid`, or use the `lo < hi` boundary template deliberately.
- **Overflow** in `(lo + hi) / 2` in Java/C++ with huge indexes. Use `lo + (hi - lo) / 2`.
- **The input must be monotone**. Binary search on unsorted data returns garbage.
- Mixing the two templates (`<=` with `hi = n`). Pick one and keep the invariant in mind.
- JS: `Math.floor((lo + hi) / 2)`, because `/` gives a float.

diagrams.title: Each step discards half the candidates
diagrams.code:
flowchart TD
  A["range of n items"] --> B["compare with middle"]
  B -- "target is smaller" --> C["keep left half: n/2"]
  B -- "target is larger" --> D["keep right half: n/2"]
  C --> E["... n/4 ... until 1"]
  D --> E

complexity.op: Search on the answer (check costs C)

keyPoints: Binary search halves the candidate range each step, so it takes O(log n) comparisons on sorted data.
Keep an invariant: the answer, if it exists, is always inside [lo, hi].
The boundary template (lo < hi, hi = mid) finds the first position where a condition turns true.
You can binary search a range of possible answers whenever 'is X enough?' is monotone.
Compute mid as lo + (hi - lo) / 2 and always move past mid to avoid infinite loops.

check.q: About how many comparisons does binary search need for 1,000,000 sorted items?
When can you binary search over the answer instead of an array?
options: When the answer is an integer
When 'is X big enough?' flips from false to true once as X increases
Only when an array is provided
check.why: Monotonic feasibility is the requirement; the search space can be a plain number range.

check.q: In the lo <= hi template, what happens if you set hi = mid instead of hi = mid - 1?
options: It can loop forever when lo == hi
check.why: When lo == hi == mid and a[mid] is not the target, hi stays the same, so the range never shrinks.
